title: On Writing History: The Historian's Duty to Truth
excerpt: What is the historian's purpose? To celebrate victors or to analyze truth? I have chosen the latter, even when it proves uncomfortable to power.
author: sallust

content.diary:
As I continue writing my historical accounts, I find myself confronted repeatedly with questions about the purpose of history and the historian's responsibilities. Should I write to celebrate Rome and her great men? Should I write to entertain and dramatic effect? Or should I attempt to write truth, even when truth is uncomfortable?

I have chosen the latter path, though it has cost me. I have written accounts of the Catilinarian Conspiracy and the Jugurthine War that cast the victors—men like Cicero and Metellus—in less flattering light than they would prefer. I have analyzed the systemic corruption of Rome's political system rather than merely celebrating individual heroes.

This approach has generated criticism. Some accuse me of bias, of allowing personal political opinions to color my historical accounts. They may be correct. I do not claim perfect objectivity. But I do claim an attempt to analyze events in context, to identify underlying causes rather than merely chronicling surface events, to distinguish between official narratives and actual complexity.

Consider how victorious generals typically narrate their campaigns. They present themselves as military geniuses whose victories resulted from their own superior judgment and courage. If their campaigns involved setbacks, the blame is placed on circumstance or on subordinates. The general emerges as hero of the narrative.

But actual military campaigns are more complex. Success typically results from multiple factors: the competence of subordinates, the courage of soldiers, luck and circumstance, the opponent's mistakes, logistical advantages, and yes, the commander's judgment. An honest historian must account for all these factors rather than attributing success to a single great man.

Similarly, when an orator like Cicero claims that he personally saved the Republic through his words and wisdom, the honest historian must examine the claim skeptically. Did Cicero's oratory actually expose facts that senators did not already suspect? Or did Cicero's words provide rhetorical justification for actions the Senate was already prepared to take? These are important distinctions that affect how we interpret what actually happened.

I have attempted in my writings to provide this kind of honest analysis. I acknowledge the genuine talents of men like Cicero and Metellus. But I do not permit my acknowledgment of their talents to blind me to the systemic problems they operated within and often perpetuated.

My approach has implications for how history should be written and read. History should be read not merely as a collection of great deeds by great men but as an analysis of how societies function, what problems they face, how underlying structures shape outcomes. A good history asks why things happened rather than merely recording what happened.

I recognize that my work will be criticized. Those whose reputations or preferred narratives are challenged by my analysis will find ways to dismiss or discredit my work. This is the fate of historians who attempt truth rather than celebration. But I believe the effort is worthwhile. Future generations deserve historical accounts that attempt to understand reality rather than merely perpetuate propaganda.

When I am gone, my accounts will remain. They will be challenged and debated. But they will provide future historians with an alternative to the self-congratulatory narratives that men like Cicero leave behind. That contribution, I believe, justifies the criticism I face.
content.scientific:
Sallust's approach to historical writing represented an important methodological development in ancient historiography. Rather than following the panegyric tradition (writing celebratory accounts of great men), Sallust attempted analytical history that examined underlying causes and systemic issues.

Sallust's method involved several characteristics:

First, he attempted to provide context for events—to explain not merely what happened but why it happened. This contextual approach suggested that historical causation was complex, involving multiple factors rather than simple monocausal explanations.

Second, he acknowledged multiple perspectives rather than presenting a single authoritative narrative. While this could be seen as a weakness (multiple perspectives create ambiguity), it represented an honest acknowledgment that historical events are complex and that different actors interpret them differently.

Third, Sallust analyzed social and structural factors alongside individual actions. Rather than attributing outcomes entirely to the wisdom or folly of great men, he examined how social structures, economic factors, and systemic problems shaped outcomes.

Fourth, Sallust was attentive to rhetorical manipulation. He recognized that powerful figures use language and narrative to frame events in ways favorable to themselves. The historian's duty, in Sallust's view, was to penetrate these rhetorical frames and understand what actually occurred.

This methodological approach proved influential. Later Roman historians and modern historians have drawn on Sallust's model when attempting to move beyond simple celebration of great men toward structural and contextual analysis.

However, scholars have also noted that Sallust's own work was not free from bias. His sympathy for Caesar and critical stance toward the conservative faction shaped his interpretations. His moral judgments about Roman corruption were genuine but also served political purposes. The lesson from Sallust's work is not that objective history is possible but that historians who attempt to understand complexity and context, while acknowledging their own biases, produce more useful historical analysis than those merely celebrating power.

quote.translation: History is the teacher of life.
quote.author: Gaius Sallustius Crispus
